sections.authorBiography: Sophocles wrote his tragedies for the festivals of Dionysus at Athens in the fifth century B.C.E. An ancient summary of Antigone says he was chosen as one of Athens' generals for the war against Samos in 440 B.C.E.; Jebb treats the tradition with care and takes it to show that Antigone was known before the summer of 441 (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 20). He wrote Oedipus at Colonus in his last years, about 406 B.C.E., and it was brought out after his death by his grandson and namesake (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). His three Theban plays were not written in story order: Antigone came first and Oedipus at Colonus last (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). This app uses Francis Storr's English verse translation (1912) as edited by Standard Ebooks; line numbers are Storr's English lines, not the Greek.
sections.historicalContext: Jebb dates the writing to Sophocles' final years, about 406 B.C.E., and reports the ancient notice that the play was brought out after the poet's death by his grandson and namesake, Sophocles son of Ariston (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). The play is set at Colonus, near Athens; the connection of Oedipus with Colonus was no invention of Sophocles (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 8). Greeks believed a hero's grave could protect a city, which is why Thebes now wants Oedipus back. Slavery was legal; Creon and Theseus use slave as an insult (lines 869, 963), and owning people was wrong.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play was staged after Sophocles' death (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). This app uses Francis Storr's 1912 verse translation; the Standard Ebooks text has transcription errors, corrected in the app against Storr's 1912 edition (Sophocles, 1912/2026).
publicationAndReception.then: Jebb reads the play as a sequel that meets Oedipus again after the lapse of several years: in the earlier play he sees only his guilt, while here he insists on his moral innocence because he acted without knowing (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 3).
publicationAndReception.now: Taught as the middle of the story, it explains how Oedipus' curse on his sons and Polyneices' request for burial (lines 1457–1463) lead into Antigone, and it ends with Antigone resolving to go back to Thebes (line 1822).

sections.overview: Blind and old, Oedipus arrives with his daughter Antigone at a sacred grove at Colonus, near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground and that he must leave, but Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that this would be his last resting place, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out.
sections.whyItMatters: The play asks what a community owes a stranger it fears, and whether a person is defined by acts done in ignorance. It also completes the story: the cursed king becomes a protector of the city that welcomed him.

spoilerOverview.text: Creon seizes the daughters; Theseus rescues them. Oedipus curses Polyneices. At the thunder Oedipus leads Theseus to the place of his passing, which only Theseus sees; it is a mystery, an end most marvellous (line 1705). Antigone resolves to return to Thebes.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” slowly and put it in my own words: In these lines Oedipus speaks at a turning point of the section, which is about the beggar at the sacred grove. Next, craft. I notice how the lines use setting, characterization to make the audience feel the pressure of the moment on Oedipus. The strongest word is “Antigone”: the word “Antigone” carries the weight of the lines and points to the section's big idea. Then, effect. What do lines 1–2 reveal about the beggar at the sacred grove? My answer: The king who once solved riddles must now ask where he is. The forbidden grove of the Furies becomes his place of rest. These lines show the beggar at the sacred grove, and that matters for what follows in the play.

segments.activity: Whole-class discussion: why the book is still taught.
segments.script: Why does Oedipus at Colonus still matter? The play is about how a ruined person can claim dignity, how a city treats refugees and suppliants, and how families carry old wrongs. It completes the story of Oedipus with mercy and a death that is a blessing rather than a punishment.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Jebb notes that the link between Oedipus and Colonus was no invention of Sophocles and that the play was staged after his death. Why might Athenians have valued a play in which Oedipus' grave protects their city? Answer: Accept answers such as: the play turns a cursed outsider into a protector of Athens, so it honours the city's own ground and its welcome of a suppliant.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Oedipus at Colonus.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Oedipus at Colonus: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Oedipus at Colonus has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to refuge and hospitality.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Oedipus at Colonus. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to refuge and hospitality.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Oedipus at Colonus.

Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the scene: “The curse makes a family's past its future. Polyneices' burial request is the seed of Antigone.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive in part. “But as almighty Zeus in all he doth / Hath Mercy for co-partner of his throne, / Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned / In thy heart likewise” (Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501), Polyneices) supports it: Polyneices asks his father's pardon and help in the war on Thebes. Oedipus curses him: the brothers will die by each other's hands. Antigone begs Polyneices to turn back; he refuses and asks his sisters to bury him if the curse comes true, which sets up Antigone. But “They tend me, they preserve me, they are men / Not women in true service to their sire; / But ye are bastards, and no sons of mine” (Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501), Oedipus) complicates it: the line (Oedipus, lines 1419–1421) shows the same issue from another side, and its “Not” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. The claim is therefore a strong reading, not a complete one, and a careful answer says where it stops applying.

Chorus, in this part of the section. The evidence is “Who craves excess of days, / Scorning the common span” (Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: "Not to be born". The words “craves” and “common” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Polyneices, lines 1479–1480. The evidence is “I shall not tell it; a good general / Reports successes and conceals mishaps” (Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501), Polyneices). This develops refuge and hospitality: Polyneices and the father's curse. The words “successes” and “conceals” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Thunder sounds. Oedipus knows his end has come and calls for Theseus. Without a guide, he leads Theseus and his daughters toward the place of his passing, and tells Theseus that the secret, passed from ruler to heir, will protect Athens. The evidence is “Time with never sleeping eye / Watches what is writ on high, / Overthrowing now the great, / Raising now from low estate” (Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 1508–1511. This develops refuge and hospitality: the summons.

Oedipus, lines 1599–1602. The evidence is “O light, no light to me, but mine erewhile, / Now the last time I feel thee palpable, / For I am drawing near the final gloom / Of Hades” (Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605), Oedipus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the summons. The words “palpable” and “erewhile” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Refuge and hospitality

Chorus, in this part of the section. The evidence is “If mortal prayers are heard in hell, / Hear, Goddess dread, invisible” (Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: a prayer for an easy death. The words “invisible” and “prayers” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

The elders pray to the powers of the underworld to let Oedipus pass gently and without pain. The evidence is “By a gentle, tearless doom / Speed this stranger to the gloom, / Let him enter without pain / The all-shrouding Stygian plain” (Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625), Chorus) — Chorus, lines 1610–1613. This develops refuge and hospitality: a prayer for an easy death.

Oedipus, lines 1–2. The evidence is “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” (Prologue (lines 1–114), Oedipus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the beggar at the sacred grove. The words “reached” and “region” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Blind and old, Oedipus arrives with Antigone at a grove near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground of the Eumenides and that he must leave. Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that he would end his days here, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out.

Near the start, “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” (Prologue (lines 1–114), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 1–2. Later, “There,’ said he, ‘shalt thou round thy weary life, / A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, / But to the land that cast thee forth,…” (Prologue (lines 1–114), Oedipus) — Oedipus, lines 91–93. The beggar at the sacred grove.

Oedipus, lines 74. The evidence is “The blind man’s words will be instinct with sight” (Prologue (lines 1–114), Oedipus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the beggar at the sacred grove. The words “instinct” and “sight” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Blind and old, Oedipus arrives with Antigone at a grove near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground of the Eumenides and that he must leave. Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that he would end his days here, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out.

Antigone, lines 243–244. The evidence is “Where will you find one, search ye ne’er so well, / Who ’scapes perdition if a god impel” (Parodos (lines 115–248), Antigone). This develops refuge and hospitality: the elders' fear. The words “perdition” and “search” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The elders of Colonus search for the trespasser. When they learn his name, they order him out. Antigone pleads for him.

Chorus, lines 222–223. The evidence is “Heaven’s justice never smites / Him who ill with ill requites” (Parodos (lines 115–248), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the elders' fear. The words “requites” and “justice” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The elders of Colonus search for the trespasser. When they learn his name, they order him out. Antigone pleads for him.

Oedipus, lines 393. The evidence is “So, when I cease to be, my worth begins” (Episode 1 (lines 249–694), Oedipus). This develops refuge and hospitality: Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome. The words “begins” and “cease” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Oedipus defends himself: he acted in self-defence and without knowledge. Ismene brings news that his sons are fighting over Thebes and that an oracle says whoever holds Oedipus' grave will prosper, so Creon is coming for him. Oedipus curses his sons, purifies the grove through Ismene, and answers the elders' questions about the incest and the killing. Theseus arrives, recalls that he too was an exile, and grants Oedipus protection.

Chorus, lines 695–698. The evidence is “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening…” (Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the Colonus ode. The words “glistening” and “goodliest” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The elders praise Colonus and Athens: the nightingale, the river Cephisus, Athena's olive, and Poseidon's gifts of the horse and the oar.

Chorus, lines 720–728. The evidence is “And here there grows, unpruned, untamed, / Terror to foemen’s spear, / A tree in Asian soil unnamed, / By Pelops’ Dorian isle unclaimed, /…” (Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the Colonus ode. The words “unclaimed” and “withering” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The elders praise Colonus and Athens: the nightingale, the river Cephisus, Athena's olive, and Poseidon's gifts of the horse and the oar.

A defended position: Chorus, lines 695–698. The evidence is “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening…” (Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the Colonus ode. The elders praise Colonus and Athens: the nightingale, the river Cephisus, Athena's olive, and Poseidon's gifts of the horse and the oar.

Creon, lines 869. The evidence is “Command your minions; I am not your slave” (Episode 2 (lines 740–1091), Creon). This develops refuge and hospitality: Creon seizes the daughters. The words “minions” and “slave” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Creon arrives with smooth words. When Oedipus refuses him, Creon reveals that his men have seized Ismene and drags off Antigone. Theseus arrives, rebukes Creon for breaking Athenian law, and sends men to rescue the girls. Creon calls Oedipus polluted; Oedipus answers that he acted unknowingly.

Chorus, lines 1134–1137. The evidence is “O for the wings, the wings of a dove, / To be borne with the speed of the gale, / Up and still upwards to sail / And gaze on the fray from…” (Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152), Chorus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the rescue imagined. The words “upwards” and “clouds” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The elders imagine the chase and the battle and pray to Zeus and Athena for victory.

Theseus, lines 1210. The evidence is “A wise man heeds all matters great or small” (Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269), Theseus). This develops refuge and hospitality: the daughters return; a suppliant son. The words “matters” and “small” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Theseus brings the daughters back. Oedipus thanks him but will not touch him, believing himself still polluted. Theseus reports that a kinsman has taken sanctuary at Poseidon's altar: Polyneices. Oedipus refuses to see him; Antigone persuades him to listen.

Oedipus, lines 1419–1421. The evidence is “They tend me, they preserve me, they are men / Not women in true service to their sire; / But ye are bastards, and no sons of mine” (Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501), Oedipus). This develops refuge and hospitality: Polyneices and the father's curse. The words “bastards” and “preserve” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Polyneices asks his father's pardon and help in the war on Thebes. Oedipus curses him: the brothers will die by each other's hands. Antigone begs Polyneices to turn back; he refuses and asks his sisters to bury him if the curse comes true, which sets up Antigone.

Messenger, lines 1657–1663. The evidence is “My children, ye will lose your sire today, / For all of me has perished, and no more / Have ye to bear your long, long ministry; / A heavy…” (Exodos (lines 1626–1831), Messenger). This develops refuge and hospitality: the mysterious passing. The words “tribulations” and “ministry” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. A messenger reports Oedipus' last farewell and his mysterious passing, seen only by Theseus. The daughters mourn. Theseus keeps his promise not to reveal the grave and promises them his care. Antigone resolves to return to Thebes.

finalPaper.title: Oedipus at Colonus: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Sophocles develops refuge and hospitality across Oedipus at Colonus. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Oedipus at Colonus and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to guilt and intent.
Analyze a central character's choices in Oedipus at Colonus. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Oedipus at Colonus finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of curse and mercy. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The king who once solved riddles must now ask where he is. The forbidden grove of the Furies becomes his place of rest. The text makes this visible when it says “Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, / What region, say, whose city have we reached” (Prologue (lines 1–114), Oedipus). Blind and old, Oedipus arrives with Antigone at a grove near Athens. A local man tells him it is holy ground of the Eumenides and that he must leave. Oedipus refuses: Apollo foretold that he would end his days here, a blessing to his hosts and a curse to the land that cast him out. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
